p.src: Now Jiang Wei, seeing Wei Yan stamp out the lamp, was filled with anger and drew his sword to kill him. Kongming stopped him, saying, “My allotted life is destined to end. This is not Wenchang’s fault.” Jiang Wei then sheathed his sword. Kongming spat several mouthfuls of blood and collapsed upon his bed. He said to Wei Yan, “Sima Yi has learned that I am ill and has therefore sent men to discover whether the report is true. Go out at once and meet the enemy.” Wei Yan received the order, left the tent and mounted his horse, then led his troops charging out of the camp. When Xiahou Ba saw Wei Yan, he hastily led his army in retreat. Wei Yan pursued him for more than twenty li before returning. Kongming ordered Wei Yan to return to his own camp and guard it.

p.src: Jiang Wei entered the tent and went straight to Kongming’s bedside to inquire after him. Kongming said, “I had wished to exhaust my loyalty and strength, recover the Central Plains, and restore the house of Han; but since Heaven wills it thus, I shall die before morning or evening has passed. All that I learned in my life I have set down in twenty-four treatises, comprising one hundred and four thousand, one hundred and twelve characters. They contain the methods of the Eight Duties, Seven Admonitions, Six Fears, and Five Dreads. I have considered all our commanders, but none is fit to receive them. You alone may inherit my writings. You must never treat them lightly!” Weeping, Jiang Wei bowed and received them. Kongming continued, “I also devised a method for the repeating crossbow, but never had the opportunity to employ it. Its bolts are eight cun long, and a single crossbow can discharge ten of them. I have drawn complete plans for it. You may construct and use it according to those plans.” Jiang Wei bowed and accepted this also. Kongming continued, “There is no need for great concern over any of the routes in Shu; only the region of Yinping must be watched with the utmost care. Though the terrain there is steep and perilous, in time it will surely be lost.” He then summoned Ma Dai into the tent, whispered in his ear, and entrusted him with a secret plan; he instructed him, “After I die, act according to this plan.” Ma Dai received the plan and departed. A short while later, Yang Yi entered. Kongming called him to the bedside, gave him a brocade bag, and secretly instructed him, “When I am dead, Wei Yan will certainly rebel. When he does, wait until you face him in battle before opening this bag. Then the man who is to slay Wei Yan will reveal himself.” After Kongming had arranged every matter, he suddenly lost consciousness and collapsed. He did not revive until evening, whereupon he submitted a memorial to the Latter Ruler that very night. The Latter Ruler was greatly alarmed upon hearing the report and urgently ordered Li Fu, Imperial Secretary, to hasten through the night to the army, inquire after Kongming, and ask about arrangements for the future. Li Fu received the command and hurried to Wuzhang Plains. He went in to see Kongming, conveyed the Latter Ruler’s message, and finished his inquiries after his health. Kongming wept and said, “Unhappily, I am to perish midway, leaving the great affairs of the state fruitlessly unfinished and becoming culpable before all under Heaven. After my death, you gentlemen must exhaust your loyalty in supporting our sovereign. The established institutions of the state must not be altered; nor should the men I appointed be lightly dismissed. I have taught all my military methods to Jiang Wei. He is capable of carrying on my aspirations and exerting himself for the state. My life may end at any moment. I shall now prepare a final memorial for submission to the Son of Heaven.” Having received these words, Li Fu hurriedly took his leave.

p.src: When Kongming had finished writing, he again instructed Yang Yi, “After I die, do not announce my death. Have a large shrine made and seat my corpse within it; place seven grains of rice in my mouth; and set one bright lamp at my feet. Keep the army as quiet as usual, and on no account raise lamentations. Then my general’s star will not fall. My departed spirit will rise and hold it in place. When Sima Yi sees that the general’s star has not fallen, he will surely become alarmed and suspicious. Order the rear camp of our army to depart first, then withdraw slowly, one camp after another. If Sima Yi comes in pursuit, draw up your battle formation, turn the standards about, and beat the drums as though advancing. When he approaches, place the wooden image of me that I had carved earlier upon a carriage, push it out before the army, and have officers and soldiers of every rank stand arrayed on either side. When Sima Yi sees it, he will surely flee in terror.” Yang Yi assented to every instruction. That night, Kongming had attendants help him outside. Looking up at the Northern Dipper, he pointed to a distant star and said, “That is my general’s star.” Everyone looked and saw that its light was dim and that it trembled as though about to fall. Kongming pointed his sword at it and recited an incantation. When the incantation was finished, he hurried back to his tent and lost consciousness. While the commanders were in confusion, Imperial Secretary Li Fu unexpectedly arrived again. Seeing Kongming unconscious and unable to speak, he wept bitterly and cried, “I have ruined a great affair of state!” Presently Kongming revived. He opened his eyes and looked around, and saw Li Fu standing before his bed. Kongming said, “I already know why you have returned.” Li Fu apologized, saying, “I was commanded by the Son of Heaven to ask who might be entrusted with the great affairs of state after the Chancellor passes away. In my haste just now, I neglected to ask, and so I have returned.” Kongming said, “After my death, the man best suited to bear responsibility for great affairs is Jiang Gongyan.” Li Fu asked, “After Gongyan, who may succeed him?” Kongming replied, “Fei Wenwei may succeed him.” Li Fu asked again, “After Wenwei, who should succeed?” Kongming made no reply. The commanders stepped forward to look and found that he had already died. It was the twenty-third day of the eighth month, in the autumn of the twelfth year of Jianxing. He was fifty-four years old. If I pursue him now, I shall surely fall into his trap.” He therefore reined in his horse and returned to camp without advancing. p.src: Meanwhile, in his own camp, Wei Yan dreamed one night that two horns had suddenly grown from his head. When he awoke, he was deeply puzzled by it. The next day, Zhao Zhi, an army administrative officer, arrived. Wei Yan invited him in and asked, “I have long known that you possess a profound understanding of the Book of Changes. Last night I dreamed that two horns grew from my head. I do not know whether this portends good or ill. Pray interpret it for me.” Zhao Zhi pondered for a long while, then replied, “It is a most auspicious sign. The qilin bears a horn upon its head, as does the azure dragon; it signifies transformation and soaring ascent.” Wei Yan was overjoyed. “If your words prove true, I shall reward you handsomely!” Zhao Zhi took his leave. Before he had gone several li, he happened to meet the Imperial Secretary Fei Yi. Fei Yi asked where he had come from. Zhao Zhi replied, “I have just come from Wei Wenchang’s camp. Wenchang dreamed that horns grew from his head and ordered me to divine whether it meant good or ill. It is in truth no auspicious omen, but fearing he would resent plain speech, I explained it in terms of the qilin and the azure dragon.” Fei Yi asked, “How do you know it is not auspicious?” Zhao Zhi replied, “The written form of the character jiao, ‘horn,’ consists of ‘knife’ above ‘use.’ Now, to use a knife upon the head is exceedingly ominous!” Fei Yi said, “Say nothing of this to anyone for now.” Zhao Zhi then departed. Fei Yi arrived at Wei Yan’s camp, dismissed all attendants, and told him, “At the third watch last night, the Chancellor passed away. With his dying breath, he repeatedly charged that you, General, should cover the rear against Sima Yi while the army withdrew slowly, and that his death was not to be announced. Here is the military tally; you may raise your troops at once.” Wei Yan asked, “Who is to assume the Chancellor’s great responsibilities?” Fei Yi replied, “The Chancellor entrusted all affairs of state to Yang Yi; and all the secret arts of warfare to Jiang Boyue. This military tally conveys Yang Yi’s command.” Wei Yan said, “Though the Chancellor is dead, I still live. Yang Yi is no more than a chief secretary. How can he bear so great a responsibility? His proper duty is merely to escort the coffin into Shu for burial. I shall personally lead the main army against Sima Yi and see that victory is won. How can the great affairs of the state be abandoned on account of the Chancellor alone?” Fei Yi said, “The Chancellor’s dying command was that we should withdraw for the present. It must not be disobeyed.” Wei Yan angrily replied, “Had the Chancellor followed my plan at the time, Chang’an would have been taken long ago! I now hold the offices of General of the Vanguard and Great General Who Conquers the West, and the title Marquis of Nanzheng. How could I consent to serve as rearguard under a mere chief secretary?” Fei Yi said, “Though what you say is reasonable, General, we must not act rashly and invite the enemy’s ridicule. Let me go and see Yang Yi, explain what is at stake, and have him yield command of the army to you. What say you?” Wei Yan agreed to his proposal.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xiahou Ba led troops to the Wuzhang Plains. Finding not a soul there, he hurried back and reported to Sima Yi, “The Shu army has withdrawn completely.” Sima Yi stamped his foot. “Kongming truly is dead! We must pursue at once!” Xiahou Ba said, “Commander, you must not pursue rashly. A subordinate general should be sent ahead first.” Sima Yi said, “This time I must go myself.” He then led his forces, together with his two sons, in a headlong charge toward the Wuzhang Plains; shouting and waving their banners, they stormed the Shu camp, only to find it utterly deserted. Sima Yi turned to his two sons and said, “Hurry the troops after me. I shall lead a force ahead.” Thus Sima Shi and Sima Zhao urged the troops onward from the rear; Sima Yi himself led the van. Reaching the foot of the mountain and seeing the Shu army not far ahead, he pressed the pursuit with all his might. Suddenly a cannon sounded behind the mountain and a tremendous shout arose. The Shu troops all wheeled their banners and turned their drums; from among the trees floated the great banner of the central army, bearing in large characters the words: “Zhuge Liang, Chancellor of Han and Marquis of Wuxiang.” Sima Yi turned pale with terror. Peering intently, he saw several dozen senior generals of the central army escorting a four-wheeled carriage into view; upon it sat Kongming upright, wearing his silk cap, holding his feather fan, and clad in a crane-feather cloak with black cords. Sima Yi cried in terror, “Kongming still lives! I have rashly entered dangerous ground and fallen into his trap!” He hastily reined his horse around and fled. Behind him Jiang Wei shouted, “Enemy general, do not flee! You have fallen into our Chancellor’s stratagem!” The Wei soldiers were terrified out of their wits. Casting away armor and helmets, spears and halberds, each fled for his life. They trampled one another, and countless men died. Sima Yi fled for more than fifty li before two Wei generals caught up from behind. Seizing his horse’s bit rings, they cried, “Do not be alarmed, Commander!” Sima Yi felt his head with his hand and asked, “Is my head still upon me?” The two generals replied, “Fear not, Commander. The Shu troops are far away.” Sima Yi panted for a long while before finally regaining his composure; opening his eyes to look, he saw that they were Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Hui; he then slowly gathered his reins and, with the two generals, took a bypath back to his own camp, while ordering the other generals to scatter their troops and scout in every direction.

shouting and waving their banners, they stormed the Shu camp, only to find it utterly deserted.
Sima Yi turned to his two sons and said, “Hurry the troops after me. I shall lead a force ahead.”
Thus Sima Shi and Sima Zhao urged the troops onward from the rear;
Sima Yi himself led the van. Reaching the foot of the mountain and seeing the Shu army not far ahead, he pressed the pursuit with all his might.

ja: かんじょうしょうたけさとこうしょかつりょう
u.src: Suddenly a cannon sounded behind the mountain and a tremendous shout arose. The Shu troops all wheeled their banners and turned their drums; from among the trees floated the great banner of the central army, bearing in large characters the words: “Zhuge Liang, Chancellor of Han and Marquis of Wuxiang.”
Sima Yi turned pale with terror.

ja: じょうしょうすうじゅうにん
u.src: Peering intently, he saw several dozen senior generals of the central army escorting a four-wheeled carriage into view;
upon it sat Kongming upright, wearing his silk cap, holding his feather fan, and clad in a crane-feather cloak with black cords.
Sima Yi cried in terror, “Kongming still lives!
I have rashly entered dangerous ground and fallen into his trap!”
He hastily reined his horse around and fled.
Behind him Jiang Wei shouted, “Enemy general, do not flee!
You have fallen into our Chancellor’s stratagem!”
The Wei soldiers were terrified out of their wits. Casting away armor and helmets, spears and halberds, each fled for his life. They trampled one another, and countless men died.
Sima Yi fled for more than fifty li before two Wei generals caught up from behind. Seizing his horse’s bit rings, they cried, “Do not be alarmed, Commander!”
Sima Yi felt his head with his hand and asked, “Is my head still upon me?”
The two generals replied, “Fear not, Commander. The Shu troops are far away.”
Sima Yi panted for a long while before finally regaining his composure;
opening his eyes to look, he saw that they were Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Hui;
he then slowly gathered his reins and, with the two generals, took a bypath back to his own camp, while ordering the other generals to scatter their troops and scout in every direction.

p.src: Two days later, some villagers came running to report, “When the Shu army withdrew into the valley, cries of mourning shook the earth, and white banners were raised throughout the host. p.src: Once Sima Yi knew for certain that Kongming was dead, he again led his troops in pursuit. When he reached Chi’an Slope, he saw that the Shu army had already gone far away, so he turned back and said to his generals, “Kongming is dead. We may all sleep soundly without fear!” He then withdrew his army and returned. Along the way, he examined the places where Kongming had pitched his camps and saw that every position—front, rear, left, and right—was arranged in perfect order and according to sound method. Sima Yi sighed, “He was truly an extraordinary genius of the realm!” Thereupon he led his forces back to Chang’an, assigning his generals separately to guard the strategic passes. Sima Yi himself returned to Luoyang for an audience with the emperor.
